quotes.text: In the book of Revelation, Alpha and Omega (Christ) promises to give freely to him who is athirst "the fountain of the water of life" (see Revelation 21:6; see also D&C 10:66). The book of Isaiah refers to the day of restoration when "with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation" (Isaiah 12:3; see also 55:1). Latter-day Church leaders often use the phrase "broken cisterns that can hold no water" in describing various fruitless practices or concepts. Elder Marion D. Hanks made this application of the expression: The substitutions we fashion to take the place of God in our lives truly hold no water. To the measure we thus refuse the "living water," we miss the joy we could have. (Conference Report, Apr. 1972, p. 127.)

quotes.text: How natural it was, then, for the Lord and his prophets to use the search for water as a pattern for the search for salvation. Just as a man is spared temporally by drinking the life-giving liquids of mortality, so he is saved eternally by downing great draughts of living water. Moses at Meribah smote the rock and a great flood of water gushed forth to give drink to all Israel and their cattle, thus teaching them that if they would look to Jehovah, by whose power the miracle was wrought, they might drink forever from streams of living water. (Num. 20:1-13.) Jeremiah proclaimed that "the Lord" was "the fountain of living waters." (Jer. 17:13.) And the Lord himself, complaining about the rebellious nature of his people, said: "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water." (Jer. 2:13.) After his resurrection this same Jehovah, identifying himself as the Lord Jesus Christ, spoke similarly to Moroni in these words: "Faith, hope and charity bringeth unto me-the fountain of all righteousness." (Ether 12:28.)

Noph . . . Tahapanes--Memphis, capital of Lower Egypt, on the west bank of the Nile, near the pyramids of Gizeh, opposite the site of modern Cairo. Daphne, on the Tanitic branch of the Nile, near Pelusium, on the frontier of Egypt towards Palestine. Isa 30:4 contracts it, Hanes. These two cities, one the capital, the other that with which the Jews came most in contact, stand for the whole of Egypt. Tahapanes takes its name from a goddess, Tphnet [CHAMPOLLION]. Memphis is from Man-nofri, "the abode of good men"; written in Hebrew, Moph (Ho 9:6), or Noph. The reference is to the coming invasion of Judah by Pharaoh-necho of Egypt, on his return from the Euphrates, when he deposed Jehoahaz and levied a heavy tribute on the land (2Ki 23:33-35). Josiah's death in battle with the same Pharaoh is probably included (2Ki 23:29, 30).

notes.text: 20-30. The second evil spoken of in verse 13, that of following after the false gods of other nations, is further described in these verses. Jehovah reminds Israel of times past when he delivered her out of bondage and she then covenanted to keep his commandments; yet on many subsequent occasions, Israel wandered astray and played the harlot by having an affair with Baal or Baalim, the false gods of the surrounding nations. Baal was worshiped in high places among groves of trees-and this included temple prostitution. Therefore, the description of Israel as a harlot carries a double meaning: a literal act of immorality and a figurative representation of Israel's forsaking her husband (Jehovah) to have an affair with another god. The Lord next declares that Israel had been planted by him as a noble vine, wholly a good seed, and asks why she has become a degenerate and strange vine to him. He further describes her apostasy as an internal or spiritual one. and her uncleanliness as that which cannot be washed away with soap or cleansing agents. Israel's or Judah's pretended impotence is refuted by the Lord. and he compares his wayward people to two familiar animals. The first is a swift dromedary which has gone against her training. A dromedary is a one-humped camel especially bred and trained for riding. Israel is therefore accused of knowingly forsaking the commandments of God. Secondly, the Lord compares her to a wild ass who has learned the way of the wilderness and is free to follow the desires of her heart. He then asks, "In her occasion who can turn her away?" The question seems to be, "Who can take away her freedom?" The King James Version of the Bible marginal note reads "or, reverse it?" The Joseph Smith Translation of the Bible (often referred to as the "Inspired Version") renders the answer, "All they that seek her will weary themselves; in her month they shall not find her" (verse 24; italics added). If she follows her natural instincts for freedom, she will not be caught. Other commentators, following the corrupted text, suggest that "on her occasion" and "in her month" refer to the male animals seeking her out in the time of her periodic breeding seasons, during which time she will be caught. The Joseph Smith Translation of the Bible (often referred to as the "Inspired Version") fits the context of the following verses better.
